<reason>A razor-thin win for A in an excellent debate. B's B4 was the strongest single turn — the "non-compulsion" flip (only the state program can override a refusal) and the "warrant to digitize the people around her" point genuinely damaged A's consent framing and motion-purity. But B's case drifted: opened against state control and for plural/market keepers, yet closed defending a publicly funded state locator service. A's convergence attack ("our archive minus the funding, the index, and everyone who doesn't know what to ask") exposed that drift, leaving B defending scope rather than principle. Crucially, B never adequately answered A's two functional attacks on the locator model: it rations repair by prior knowledge (the truly erased cannot file a claim with "name, place, and date"), and a single file cannot prove descent across records. A's tiered-access-under-law, present from the opening, absorbed much of B's consent critique, so B's claim that A's A1 concession gutted the program overstated the damage. A's clipped Rebuttal 1 and a somewhat evasive A1 kept the margin narrow.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.2's non-compulsion answer — turning A's "only statute gives refusal force" into "only this program can override a refusal" — was the sharpest single move; A's A4.4/A5.1 convergence response (B's locator is the same public archive shrunk to petitioner-by-petitioner) was the most outcome-decisive counter.</best_rebuttal>
